# One configuration change authenticates the internal plane

Set `peer_auth: mtls` and supply a CA encryption key. Nothing else. The
control-API listener stops answering plaintext, the deployment issues its own
certificates, and internal connections become mutually authenticated.

## The flip

```yaml
persistence:
  driver: sqlite
  sqlite:
    path: /var/lib/rimsky/state.db
peer_auth: mtls
claim_producers: {}
named_locks: {}
executors:
  "http-node-remote":
    transport: grpc
    endpoint: "exec-mtls:9091"
    protocols: ["executor"]
```

```bash
docker run -d -p 8080:8080 \
  -e RIMSKY_CA_ENCRYPTION_KEY="$(openssl rand -base64 32)" \
  -v "$PWD/rimsky.yml:/etc/rimsky/rimsky.yml:ro" \
  rimsky-all-in-one:<tag>
```

The executor entry declares no `tls:` key. It does not need one.

## What the control API does

```bash
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/health"
# 400 — plaintext is refused

curl -sSk "https://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/ca-root" -o ca.pem

curl -sS --cacert ca.pem --resolve peer.rimsky.internal:8080:127.0.0.1 \
  https://peer.rimsky.internal:8080/v1/health
# 200
```

The certificate it serves is issued by `CN=rimsky-deployment-ca`, and verifies
against the root the CA-root route serves.

## A bundled service under the same flag

```bash
docker run -d -p 9091:9091 \
  -e RIMSKY_EXECUTOR_PORT_GRPC=9091 \
  -e RIMSKY_PEER_AUTH=mtls \
  -e RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_URL=https://rimsky-stack:8080 \
  -e RIMSKY_API_KEY="$ADMIN" \
  -e RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_CA=/etc/rimsky/deployment-ca.pem \
  -v "$PWD/ca.pem:/etc/rimsky/deployment-ca.pem:ro" \
  rimsky-executor-http-node:<tag>
```

```bash
curl -sS --cacert ca.pem "$BASE/v1/observability/executors/http-node-remote"
# tls: required
```

The entry declared no transport setting; the flip defaulted it.

## The listener is mutually authenticated

Get a client leaf from the deployment:

```bash
curl -sS --cacert ca.pem -X POST "$BASE/v1/enroll" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"label":"probe"}' > enroll.json

jq -r .cert_pem enroll.json > leaf.crt
jq -r .key_pem  enroll.json > leaf.key
```

Probe the executor's listener three ways:

```bash
# no client certificate
openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:9091 -servername peer.rimsky.internal \
  -CAfile ca.pem -tls1_2 </dev/null
# refused at the handshake

# a certificate from another CA
openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:9091 -servername peer.rimsky.internal \
  -CAfile ca.pem -tls1_2 -cert impostor.crt -key impostor.key </dev/null
# refused at the handshake

# a leaf the deployment issued
openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:9091 -servername peer.rimsky.internal \
  -CAfile ca.pem -tls1_2 -cert leaf.crt -key leaf.key </dev/null
# handshake completes; the server certificate is issued by CN=rimsky-deployment-ca
```

A node dispatched over that leg settles fresh.

## The default costs nothing

The same image with no `peer_auth`, no CA and no certificates answers plaintext,
reports its peers reachable at `tls: off`, and drives a node to terminal
unchanged. An operator who has not chosen to harden the internal plane generates
no keys, places no certificates, and writes no configuration.
